questions.q: Why does this lesson describe running out of time badly as one of the most avoidable ways a presentation underperforms?
options: Because it's almost entirely a matter of planning and rehearsal, not technical architecture skill, unlike design quality itself
Because review boards never actually enforce time limits
Because time mismanagement is impossible to avoid no matter how well prepared someone is
Because only weak designs ever run over their allotted time
questions.explain: A candidate who spends too much time on context and too little on load-bearing decisions hasn't failed at architecture -- they've failed at pacing, which is a planning and rehearsal problem, largely avoidable with preparation.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend instead of continuously staring at the clock during a presentation?
options: Ignoring time entirely and focusing only on content
Checking the clock at a few deliberate checkpoints tied to the time budget, rather than continuously, to stay aware without the awareness itself becoming a distraction
Asking the board to announce the remaining time out loud every few minutes
Setting a visible timer that beeps every minute
questions.explain: Continuous clock-watching pulls focus and reads as anxious. A few deliberate checkpoints (roughly a third through, roughly two-thirds through) keep awareness without becoming a distraction.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the right triage question to ask when you realize partway through that you're running behind schedule?
options: "How do I speed up?" -- deliver every planned section at double speed
"What's the highest-value content for the time I actually have left?" -- deciding what to compress or cut rather than rushing everything equally
"Should I stop the presentation entirely?"
"How can I blame the board for taking too much time with questions?"
questions.explain: The useful triage question prioritizes value over raw speed -- skipping a planned example, compressing a tradeoff discussion, or cutting a section entirely are better choices than uniformly rushing through all planned content.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say rushing proportionally through everything is backwards under time pressure?
options: Because it means the most important, load-bearing content gets the same compressed treatment as the least important supporting detail, instead of protecting time for what matters most
Because proportional rushing is always faster than targeted cuts
Because boards prefer presentations that run over time rather than finish early
Because load-bearing decisions should always be covered last, not first
questions.explain: The better instinct is protecting time for the two or three load-bearing decisions even if it means cutting a less important section entirely -- a board that sees this deliberate call reads it as good judgment under pressure.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how does Salesforce's CTA review board reportedly treat time saved during the presentation phase?
options: Saved time is simply lost and has no effect on the rest of the session
Saved time rolls over and is added to the Q&A phase, so an efficient presentation can buy more time for direct questioning
Saved time results in an automatic deduction from the candidate's final score
Candidates are penalized for finishing a presentation early
questions.explain: Training sources describe the CTA board's presentation phase as having a fixed window where saved time rolls into the Q&A phase rather than being lost -- reframing efficient pacing as actively buying more time for questioning, not just avoiding running over.
